{{Short description|Technique and research method within computational imaging}}

'''Differentiable imaging''' is a method within [[computational imaging]] that incorporates [[differentiable programming]] to design imaging systems. It treats the entire imaging process - from light passing through optical components to the numerical reconstruction—as a differentiable programming problem. This approach links optical hardware with numerical reconstruction, enabling joint optimization of both parts through differentiable programming.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Chen |first1=Ni |last2=Cao |first2=Liangcai |last3=Poon |first3=Ting-Chung |last4=Lee |first4=Byoungho |last5=Lam |first5=Edmund Y. |date=2023-03-23 |title=Differentiable Imaging: A New Tool for Computational Optical Imaging |url=https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/apxr.202200118 |journal=Advanced Physics Research |language=en |volume=2 |issue=6 |article-number=2200118 |doi=10.1002/apxr.202200118  |doi-access=free|issn=2751-1200|hdl=10754/686576 |hdl-access=free }}</ref> Differentiable imaging additionally extends the scope of computational imaging beyond image reconstruction, such as by aiding in characterization of optical components.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Chen |first1=Ni |last2=Brady |first2=David J. |author2-link=David J. Brady |last3=Lam |first3=Edmund Y. |date=2025-07-04 |title=Differentiable Imaging: Progress, Challenges, and Outlook |journal=Advanced Devices & Instrumentation |volume=6 |article-number=0117 |doi=10.34133/adi.0117 |bibcode=2025AdDI....6..117C |doi-access=free |author-link3=Edmund Lam}}</ref>

== Background ==
{{Further|Computational imaging}}
[[Computational imaging]] combines optical hardware and computational algorithms to capture and reconstruct information that conventional imaging system cannot. This is achieved from a combination of the imaging system and the software used in the image reconstruction.<ref name=":0">{{Cite journal |last1=Mait |first1=Joseph N. |last2=Euliss |first2=Gary W. |last3=Athale |first3=Ravindra A. |date=2018-06-30 |title=Computational imaging |url=https://opg.optica.org/abstract.cfm?URI=aop-10-2-409 |journal=Advances in Optics and Photonics |language=en |volume=10 |issue=2 |pages=409 |doi=10.1364/AOP.10.000409 |bibcode=2018AdOP...10..409M |issn=1943-8206|url-access=subscription }}</ref> Since the captured information may not directly show the image of the target, these systems often rely on numerical models that describe how light encodes the target. In practice, such models may deviate from the physical systems due to uncertainties such as noise, misalignments, manufacturing imperfections, environmental variations, etc. These uncertainties can cause a mismatch between the physical system and its numerical model, which may degrade reconstruction quality and limit the effectiveness of the hardware–software co-design.<ref name=":0" /> [[Uncertainty quantification]] is also studied in other hybrid physical–numerical systems, such as [[digital twin]].<ref>{{Cite book |url=https://doi.org/10.17226/26894 |title=Foundational Research Gaps and Future Directions for Digital Twins |date=2024-03-28 |publisher=National Academies Press |isbn=978-0-309-70042-9 |location=Washington, D.C. |doi=10.17226/26894 |pmid=39088664}}</ref> While numerical modeling imaging systems date back to the several decades, such as the [[multislice]] method in [[Electron microscope|electron microscopy]]<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Cowley |first1=J. M. |last2=Moodie |first2=A. F. |date=1957-10-01 |title=The scattering of electrons by atoms and crystals. I. A new theoretical approach |url=https://journals.iucr.org/paper?S0365110X57002194 |journal=Acta Crystallographica |volume=10 |issue=10 |pages=609–619 |doi=10.1107/S0365110X57002194 |bibcode=1957AcCry..10..609C |issn=0365-110X|url-access=subscription }}</ref> or X-Ray [[nanotomography]],<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Du |first1=Ming |last2=Nashed |first2=Youssef S. G. |last3=Kandel |first3=Saugat |last4=Gürsoy |first4=Doğa |last5=Jacobsen |first5=Chris |date=2020-03-27 |title=Three dimensions, two microscopes, one code: Automatic differentiation for x-ray nanotomography beyond the depth of focus limit |journal=Science Advances |language=en |volume=6 |issue=13 |article-number=eaay3700 |doi=10.1126/sciadv.aay3700 |issn=2375-2548 |pmc=7101216 |pmid=32258397 |arxiv=1905.10433 |bibcode=2020SciA....6.3700D }}</ref> differentiable imaging emphasizes jointly modeling uncertainties and solving inverse problems with image reconstruction simultaneously.
[[File:Differentiable imaging.png|thumb|612x612px|Differentiable Imaging and Computational Imaging]]

Differentiable imaging transforms the traditional encoding model <math display="inline">y=f(x)</math> into a more comprehensive formulation <math display="inline">y=f(x, \theta)</math>, where <math>\theta</math> represents a parameter set of mismatches between physical systems and numerical models.

The forward model captures the entire imaging pipeline through a series of interconnected component functions:

<math>y = f(x, \theta), \qquad f = f_{noise} \circ f_c \circ f_{oc} \circ f_x \circ f_{oi} \circ f_i,</math>

where the function composition operator <math>\circ</math> connects each system component, and <math>\theta = \{ \theta_c, \theta_{oc}, \ldots \}</math> encompasses uncertainty system parameters. Each component corresponds to specific physical processes within the imaging system, from illumination through object interactions to sensor behavior and noises.

This forward model enables the formulation of an [[inverse problem]] that simultaneously optimizes system parameters while reconstructing images:

<math>x^*, \theta^* = \text{argmin}_{x, \theta} \mathcal{L}(f(x, \theta), y) + \sum_{n=1}^N \beta_n \mathcal{R}_n(x) </math>

<math>s.t. \quad x \in \Omega_x, \theta \in \Omega_{\theta}</math>

Here, <math>\mathcal{L}(f(x, \theta), y)</math> represents the fidelity term that quantifies the discrepancy between the model predictions and measured data.

The whole process of the <math>y=f(x, \theta)</math> is constructed as a computer graph based on differentiable programming, and the inverse problem is solved with gradient based algorithm, while the gradient is calculated with [[automatic differentiation]].

== Applications ==
One application of differentiable imaging is uncertainty management, which seeks to quantify and mitigate the impact of factors induce reality-numerical mismatch. Explicitly accounting for uncertainties can improve reconstruction accuracy and system robustness. Examples include:

* Model-related uncertainties: unknown or unmeasurable variables—for instance, optical system quantities that differ from the design specifications<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Chen |first1=Ni
